title: Chi-boundedness of graphs containing no cycles with $k$ chords: finding a cycle with exactly $k$ chords from a large collection of induced $K_{\ell,\ell}$
author: Joonkyung Lee, Shoham Letzter, Alexey Pokrovskiy
work: Chi-boundedness of graphs containing no cycles with $k$ chords
difficulty_reason: Counted unit: the article's Lemma (source0.tex lines 1189--1191, source label lem:find-cycle-from-Kll-exact): for $p,\ell\gg k\gg 1$, if a $p$-extraction of $G$ contains $\ell$ pairwise vertex-disjoint induced copies of $K_{\ell,\ell}$ with no edges between them, then $G$ has a cycle with exactly $k$ chords; delivered with the article's complete original proof at source0.tex lines 1193--1372 (180 lines, one adjacent proof environment that opens and closes inside the retained span). The lemma is the technical heart of the article's main theorem: the introduction announces that every graph with no cycle with exactly $k$ chords is $\chi$-bounded with a bounding function $f_k$, the proof of that theorem reduces to producing such a cycle from a large induced matching-like configuration of complete bipartite graphs, and the article's subsection introducing the lemma presents it as the final and most delicate step ("the much more careful analysis of the interaction between a single $K_{\ell,\ell}$, and a collection of parents, `grandparents' and `great-grandparents' of its vertices"), splitting the argument into three cases that correspond to the six cases of the article's case-analysis lemma. The proof is complete and closed inside the retained span: it sets up the three cases (a)--(f) of the case lemma, then handles the easy case by building the 20-block cycle $\C(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_{20})$ and counting its chords exactly (the $\alpha_i^2$ chords contributed by each $Q_i^*$, the chords between $\{u_{i,1},u_{i,2}\}$ and $X_i\cup Y_i$, the at most $120^2$ chords inside the blocks, and the $O(\sqrt k)$ chords inside the paths $P_{i,j}$ coming from the two retained $K_{\ell,\ell}$-to-path lemmas), and then handles the two annoying cases by building the 100-block and 80-block cycles with their gadgets and adjusting the chord counts by $3\tau$ so as to hit exactly $k$; every estimate needed for the count is either proved in line or quoted from a retained statement. The argument is long, case-heavy and technical in a way that is characteristic of research-level extremal graph theory rather than of textbook exercises. H2: an original research lemma with a complete author proof, of substantial length, resting on several quoted lemmas of the same article and of cited papers.
